extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary critics, and students of poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for composing and judging poetry and drama (especially tragedy and epic): medium, plot, character, diction, thought, spectacle, and practical composition rules derived from Aristotle's Poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the principle of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and related arts are modes of imitation (μίμησις); they differ according to the medium, the objects, and the manner of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediums of imitation are rhythm, language, and harmony (melody), taken singly or in combination. Recognize which medium your work primarily uses and how that shapes its techniques and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium, Objects, and Manner (threefold distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish arts by (1) medium (rhythm, language, harmony), (2) objects (types of persons/actions represented; higher or lower), and (3) manner (dramatic enactment, pure narrative, or mixed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the threefold distinction to decide form and style (e.g., tragic drama uses language + rhythm + spectacle differently from epic narrative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: higher vs lower types
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry represents persons of various ranks and moral qualities; the choice of higher or lower types underpins genres such as tragedy (higher) and comedy (lower).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select characters whose social/moral stature fits the intended genre and the emotional aims (pity/fear for tragedy, ridicule for comedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: dramatic vs narrative forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry can be dramatic (characters acting and speaking), pure narrative (telling), or mixed; drama is enacted, narrative is recited or told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the manner consistent with the effect: drama achieves immediacy and concentrated unity; epic narrative allows length and multiple actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the ludicrous (comic principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy (the ludicrous) arises from representations of characters and situations judged lesser or ridiculous; it has distinct origins and techniques from tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing comic material, emphasise incongruity and the representation of inferior or ludicrous types rather than tragic grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six elements of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy consists of six constituents: Spectacle (ὄψις), Song/Lyrical element (μελοποιία), Diction (λέξις), Plot (μῦθος), Character (ἦθος), and Thought (διάνοια).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is primary, followed by character and thought; spectacle, song, and diction are important but subordinate. Evaluate a tragedy by assessing each element and their integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (μῦθος)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot—the representation of action—is of chief importance in tragedy; character and thought are next in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good plot must be coherent and causally structured; when judging or composing, prioritise the integrity and configuration of events over isolated speeches or ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole (unity/complete structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be a whole, with a beginning, middle, and end, and of adequate magnitude (not too short or too long).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure completeness: the beginning admits of no prior incidents in the poem's action; the end follows necessarily from preceding events. Maintain appropriate length to preserve concentrated effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic unity consists in unity of action—one main action—rather than unity of the hero's person alone; subsidiary incidents must relate to the main action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid multiple disconnected subplots; every episode should contribute causally to the central action and outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic connection of parts / rule of probable or necessary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts must be organically connected by probable or necessary sequence; incidents should follow from one another rather than being randomly juxtaposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct causally-linked events; use probability/necessity to justify transitions. Beware sequences that violate poetic (universal) truth even if historically possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragic effects depend on combining the inevitable (necessary outcome) with the unexpected (surprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange the plot so that outcomes feel both necessary in retrospect and yet surprising when they occur (e.g., using peripeteia/anagnorisis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple plots involve change without reversal/recognition; complex plots include peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) and produce a more moving effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide complexity according to emotional aims: complex plots can yield stronger catharsis but require tighter causal construction to avoid implausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia is a change from one state to its opposite, e.g., good fortune to bad, arising naturally from the plot's structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals that are causally motivated within the plot rather than arbitrary turns; illustrate with examples (e.g., Sophocles' Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is the change from ignorance to knowledge, often coupled with reversal, producing strong tragic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recognitions to arise plausibly from events and relationships already established; different kinds of recognition (by tokens, signs, inference) are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos (πάθος) / Tragic incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathos denotes suffering or disastrous incident that evokes pity and fear; it should be integral to the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that suffering follows inevitably from the plot and character choices, and that it contributes to catharsis rather than mere sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (prologue, episodes, choral odes, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is composed of parts—prologue, episodes, choral odes, exodus—each having a function in the quantitative structure of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange parts so they contribute to the unity and unfolding of the action; avoid interpolations that disrupt causal flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic action requires a change of fortune and appropriate hero character
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal tragic action involves a change of fortune (often for the worse) experienced by a person not wholly virtuous nor wicked but appropriate to eliciting pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select protagonists whose moral stature and actions make their fall credible and moving—neither perfect nor base, but capable of error and suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for an unhappy ending as truly tragic
rubrics_metrics.description: An unhappy ending that follows from the plot is more truly tragic than 'poetic justice' or merely happy resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for tragic effect, allow consequences to follow naturally; avoid contrived happy endings that dilute catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear should arise from the plot itself, not from spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The emotions of pity and fear must spring from the incidents and structure of the plot; relying on scenic spectacle to produce them is contrary to the spirit of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute scenic effects for dramatic causes; evaluate whether emotions are organically generated by the story rather than manufactured by visual display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ἦθος): moral purpose and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Character manifests moral purpose; ethical portraiture must be probable or necessary within the plot; character is subordinate to plot but essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose decisions and moral motives are consistent and probable, serving the causal structure of the plot. Avoid irrational or gratuitous vice unless artfully justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Deus ex Machina and unjustified contrivances
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolutions introduced from outside the plot (deus ex machina) are condemned when they are irrelevant to the internal necessities of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve conflicts through internal causes and character choices; use external devices only when they can be shown to be poetically necessary and probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rules for the tragic poet: embodiment and rehearsal
rubrics_metrics.description: Poet should place the scene before his eyes and act parts himself to enter vividly into the dramatis personae; sketch the bare outline of action before composing episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with theatrical imagination—visualise scenes and enact beats; plan the skeleton of the plot prior to detailed composition to preserve unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful management of complication (δέσις) and dénouement (λύσις)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special care is required in arranging the complication and especially the denouement to ensure they follow necessarily and produce proper catharsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design causally coherent complications and ensure the denouement resolves the central action plausibly; weak denouement undermines tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite varied forms of poetic excellence; avoid epic overloading
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should, when possible, unite varied poetic excellences (plot, character, thought, diction, song, spectacle) but must not be overcharged with details proper to epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for integration of strengths; avoid inserting long epic-style digressions or excessive detail that dilute tragic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choral odes must be organic
rubrics_metrics.description: Choral odes (chorus) should be an organic part of the whole, integrated into action and not a superfluous insertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choral passages to advance theme, mood, or connect episodes; ensure they relate causally or thematically to the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (διάνοια) as intellectual element revealed through rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (reasoning, themes, arguments) is expressed in dramatic speeches and should follow rules of rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft speeches to reveal characters' beliefs and arguments; use rhetorical principles to make thought intelligible and persuasive within dramatic context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Poetic diction (λέξις): metaphor, elevation, and perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction concerns word choice and expression; poetic diction admits metaphors and requires a balance of elevation (high style) with perspicuity (clarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose language fitting to character and genre; use metaphor where apt but avoid obscure or needlessly ornate phrasing that impedes understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of grammatical forms, meters, and appropriate modes of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic language should employ suitable grammatical constructions and meters (e.g., epic meter for epic poetry) and modes of speech appropriate to characters and scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match linguistic registers to character types and medium; meter and form should serve the imitation and emotional aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth (universal) vs historical truth (particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry expresses the universal (what is generally true of human action) rather than mere particular historical fact; poetic necessity/probability governs sequence rather than strict factual chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise universal plausibility and moral/causal truth over literal factuality when shaping events; justify departures from historical detail by appeal to the poem's expressive aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling impossibility and plausibility (critical objections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impossible events must be justified by artistic requirements or common opinion; a probable impossibility is preferable to an improbable possibility for artistic ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including unlikely or impossible elements, provide artistic justification (idealisation, exemplarity) or grounds in accepted belief so the audience accepts them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between epic and tragic modes (length, metre, unity, plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and tragedy agree in unity of action but differ in length, metre, and means of producing plausibility; epic can be longer and cover multiple actions, while tragedy concentrates effect and unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose mode according to aims: epic suits extended narratives with multiple episodes; tragedy suits concentrated, unified action producing intense catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for artistic superiority (audience, vividness, concentrated effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher mode appeals to better audiences, achieves more vividness (through music/spectacle and reading), and attains its end in narrower bounds producing a concentrated pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mode or work by its capacity to produce the proper pleasure for its art: depth of effect, unity, and suitability for a refined audience indicate superiority.
